{"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "Does online political hostility on X/Twitter go with political engagement and its antecedents, not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations?", "quotes": [{"text": "We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.", "page": 2}]}],
"central_claim": [{"claim": "Online political hostility is positively associated with political engagement and its antecedents, most strongly with political interest, political knowledge and online participation.", "quotes": [{"text": "Online political hostility is positively associated with these indicators, with the strongest associations for political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.", "page": 1}]}],
"evidence": [{"claim": "The study combines two years of panel survey responses with behavioral data scraped from the X accounts of survey respondents recruited through YouGov's US web panel.", "quotes": [{"text": "Combining two years of survey and behavioral data from X/Twitter, we examine associations between online political hostility and indicators of political engagement and its antecedents among American users.", "page": 1}, {"text": "The total number of panelists where we were able to link survey responses to their X handle in this period was 2567.", "page": 6}]}, {"claim": "The corpus is about 9.25 million posts from panelists collected between March 2019 and January 2021, aggregated to the individual level.", "quotes": [{"text": "During this period, we managed to scrape 9,250,180 posts from our panelists.", "page": 6}]}, {"claim": "The primary hostility measure is a word-embedding score (the Super-Unsupervised approach) that computes each post's similarity to a 'political hate' vector, averaged per user; it was checked against 2,469 hand-labeled posts.", "quotes": [{"text": "Our key measure of online political hostility is based on a word embeddings approach termed the Super-Unsupervised (SU) approach [60].", "page": 6}, {"text": "The SU approach was also validated against 2,469 hand-labeled posts rated by four expert raters", "page": 7}]}],
"key_findings": [{"claim": "Online political hostility is positively and significantly associated with the engagement indicators and antecedents (education, efficacy, interest, knowledge, online and offline participation), after controlling for Big Five traits, income, age, gender and party identification.", "quotes": [{"text": "Fig 1 demonstrate positive and statistically significant associations between online political hostility and several indicators of political engagement and its antecedents (consistent with Expectation 1).", "page": 11}]}, {"claim": "The associations hold across the alternative hostility measures (the component words, a supervised classifier, AFINN and Perspective API), though they are largest for the primary measure.", "quotes": [{"text": "The robustness analyses are broadly consistent with the main pattern, with significant and sizeable associations across all three measures.", "page": 12}]}, {"claim": "The engagement–hostility association is more often significant among users high in leader-directed affective polarization, but the moderation evidence is uneven across indicators.", "quotes": [{"text": "for those low on affective polarization only four out of eighteen associations, across our three measures of online hostility, are significant, whereas for those high on affective polarization fourteen out of eighteen are significant.", "page": 13}]}, {"claim": "In within-person panel models, increases in online political engagement are followed by higher online political hostility, with weaker and less consistent evidence of the reverse direction.", "quotes": [{"text": "within-person increases in online political engagement are followed by higher levels of online political hostility across the three hostility measures.", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "Exploratory count models show that more hostile users post more and have more followers and, to a lesser extent, more friends.", "quotes": [{"text": "The count-model results indicate that higher political hostility is associated with more posts and with larger numbers of followers and, to a lesser extent, friends.", "page": 15}]}],
"scope_and_limits": [{"claim": "The authors say the findings do not establish that engagement causes hostility, and that the results are associational rather than causal.", "quotes": [{"text": "At the same time, our evidence does not establish that engagement causes hostility.", "page": 15}, {"text": "The findings should overall be interpreted as associational rather than causal.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "The activity and reach results are not evidence of formal network influence or centrality, and the study does not adjudicate between the grievance and personality literatures.", "quotes": [{"text": "These results suggest greater activity and potential reach, but they should not be interpreted as evidence of formal network influence or centrality.", "page": 15}, {"text": "The present study does not seek to adjudicate between these literatures.", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "The affective polarization measure covers only feelings toward party leaders, not parties or ordinary supporters, and the Big Five controls cannot test Dark Triad or sadism accounts.", "quotes": [{"text": "our measure of affective polarization captures feelings toward party elites rather than toward parties as institutions or ordinary party supporters, as is standard [22].", "page": 16}, {"text": "the utilized Big Five controls do not directly test personality-based accounts centered on more antisocial traits such as Dark Triad traits, sadism, or other antagonistic traits.", "page": 16}]}],
"theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The authors place the paper within the revisionist view of political engagement, which holds that engagement has costs as well as benefits, and extend it to online hostility and to the social media context.", "quotes": [{"text": "We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.", "page": 2}, {"text": "Here, we extend and integrate the study of the negative side of political engagement into the study of online politics with a specific focus on online political hostility.", "page": 4}]}],
"interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "The political information processing literature (e.g., Leeper and Slothuus; Taber and Lodge) argues that engaged citizens evaluate attitude-congruent and attitude-incongruent political arguments differently, and the authors build on this by applying the idea to hostility.", "quotes": [{"text": "the literature on political information processing has argued and found that indicators of political engagement (e.g., partisanship) can be associated with biased assessments of political arguments and news", "page": 4}]}]}}
